title: Variables
description: Understand what variables are, how to declare them, naming conventions, the var keyword, constants, and best practices for storing data in C#.

data.text: Every C# program works with data — numbers, text, dates, and more. **Variables** are named containers that hold this data in memory while your program runs. Think of them as labeled boxes: each box has a name, a type (what can go inside), and a value (what's currently inside).

When you create a variable, the computer reserves a small area of memory and gives it the name you chose. From that point on, you can read or change the value stored there by referring to the variable name in your code. Understanding variables is the foundation for everything else in C#.

A variable has three essential parts: a **name** (identifier), a **type** (what kind of data it holds), and a **value** (the actual data). For example, `int age = 30;` creates a variable named `age` of type `int` with the value `30`. The C# compiler uses the type to know how much memory to allocate and what operations are valid on that data.

terms.definition: A named memory location that stores a value of a specific type during program execution.
The act of telling the compiler about a variable's name and type before using it.
Assigning an initial value to a variable at the time of declaration.
The name given to a variable, method, class, or other program element.
A fixed value written directly in code, such as `42`, `"Hello"`, or `true`.

data.text: In C#, you declare a variable by writing its type followed by its name. You can optionally assign a value at the same time (called initialization). Variables that are declared but not initialized contain default values — for numeric types it's `0`, for `bool` it's `false`, and for reference types it's `null`.

data.title: Unassigned Variables
data.text: C# does NOT allow reading a local variable before it has been assigned a value. The compiler will give you an error. Class-level fields get a default value automatically, but local variables inside methods do not.

The `var` keyword lets the compiler infer the variable's type from the value on the right side. It is still **statically typed** — the type is locked in at compile time and cannot change. `var` is not the same as `dynamic`.

data.title: Using var
When to Use var
data.text: Use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side (e.g., `var list = new List<string>()`). Avoid it when the type is unclear (e.g., `var result = GetData()`), as it reduces readability for other developers.

C# developers follow well-established naming conventions so that code is readable and consistent across projects. Following these conventions makes your code easier for others (and your future self) to understand.

data.title: Rules for Naming Variables
items: Start with a letter or underscore (`_`) — never with a digit
Use only letters, digits, and underscores — no spaces or special characters
Avoid C# keywords like `class`, `int`, `return` — use `@class` if absolutely necessary
Stick to English for maximum compatibility with tools and libraries

data.text: When a value should never change, use `const` or `readonly`. A `const` variable is evaluated at compile time and must be assigned when declared. A `readonly` field is evaluated at runtime and can be assigned either at declaration or inside a constructor.

data.title: const vs readonly

cards.title: const
cards.description: Compile-time constant. Value baked into every assembly that references it.
cons: Only works with primitive or string literals
Value is baked into referencing assemblies

cards.title: readonly
cards.description: Runtime constant. Can be assigned in declaration or constructor.
pros: Can hold reference types like Guid, DateTime
cons: Only for instance or static fields

data.title: Default Values
data.text: Every type has a default value. For value types like int, bool, and double, it's 0, false, or 0.0. For reference types like string and arrays, it's null. Uninitialized local variables are NOT given a default — the compiler prevents you from reading them before assignment.

data.title: Exercise: Declare Your First Variables
data.description: Create a small program that demonstrates variable declaration, initialization, and naming conventions.
steps: Create a new console application with `dotnet new console`
Inside `Main`, declare a string variable called `studentName` and set it to your name
Declare an `int` called `score` and assign it a value between 0 and 100
Declare a `bool` called `hasPassed` and set it based on whether score >= 60
Use `var` to declare a `double` called `gpa` with a value like 3.75
Print all variables using string interpolation
Change `score` to a new value and print again to confirm variables are mutable
data.expectedOutcome: A console program that declares, initializes, and updates variables, printing formatted output using string interpolation.

items.question: What happens if I use a variable before assigning it?
items.answer: The C# compiler will give you error CS0165: 'Use of unassigned local variable'. You must assign a value before reading it.

items.question: Is var the same as dynamic?
items.answer: No. `var` is statically typed — the type is determined at compile time and cannot change. `dynamic` skips compile-time checking and resolves types at runtime.

items.question: Can I change a const value later?
items.answer: No. `const` values are immutable by design. If you need a value that can be set once at runtime, use `readonly` instead.

items.question: Should I always use var?
items.answer: No. Use `var` when the type is clear from the initializer. Use explicit types when the type is not obvious, to improve readability.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Variables are named containers that hold typed data
Declare with `type name = value` or use `var` for inference
Local variables must be assigned before reading
Use camelCase for local variables, PascalCase for constants
Use `const` for compile-time constants, `readonly` for runtime ones
Use meaningful names that describe the data
data.takeaway: Variables are the building blocks of every C# program. Declare them clearly, name them well, and use const or readonly for values that should never change.
